items.title: Human-Centric Trust Calibration and Adaptive Explainability in AI-Driven Security Operations
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in Security Operations Centers (SOCs) to support intrusion detection and threat investigation. However, accurate predictions and explainable outputs do not necessarily lead to appropriate human reliance: analysts may over-rely on incorrect recommendations or unnecessarily reject reliable ones. This work proposes a human-centric trust-calibrated framework that integrates an AI-driven Network Intrusion Detection System (NIDS), online estimation of analyst trust and cognitive load, and adaptive explanation selection within a closed-loop security interface. The NIDS combines traffic and textual threat representations to provide threat predictions, calibrated reliability estimates, and semantic evidence. Behavioral and interaction signals are processed through a probabilistic state-space model to estimate the analyst state, while a reliability-aware controller dynamically adjusts explanation depth and evidence granularity according to the Trust-Calibration Error (TCE), which captures the mismatch between inferred analyst trust and current NIDS reliability. Rather than treating trust estimation or calibration as standalone objectives, we investigate whether their integration improves operational human–AI performance under varying NIDS reliability. A controlled SOC-oriented evaluation compares the proposed trust-calibrated policy with static and trust-agnostic adaptive explanation strategies in terms of analyst decision quality, inappropriate reliance, investigation efficiency, and cognitive workload. Empirical evaluation across 2160 trials with 36 participants demonstrates that the proposed trust-calibrated policy improves decision accuracy from 81.4% to 89.3%, corresponding to an increase of 7.9 percentage points, curtails Automation Bias Rate (ABR) from 43.1% to 22.2% (31/72 to 16/72, representing a 48.4% relative reduction; GLMM-adjusted: 21.8%, a 49.4% reduction), and decreases Inappropriate Rejection Rate (IRR) from 18.8% to 11.0% (122/648 to 71/648, representing a 41.8% relative reduction; GLMM-adjusted: 18.9% to 10.9%, a 42.3% reduction), while lowering trust miscalibration error from 0.184 to 0.101. Crucially, these reliance gains are accompanied by a reduction in subjective workload from 58.4 to 48.7 on the NASA-TLX scale and a decrease in mean investigation time from 30.2 s to 28.1 s. These findings indicate that effective human-centered security interfaces should not maximize trust or explanation richness, but dynamically promote reliance that is consistent with the actual competence of the AI system.

items.title: Implicit Algorithm Aversion: How Consumer Characteristics Shape Perceptions of Ads Designed by Undisclosed AI Versus Human Advertising Professionals
items.abstract: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has profoundly reshaped the marketing landscape, providing scalable efficiencies in ad creation. However, the consumer side of AI integration remains underexplored. Drawing on algorithm aversion theory, this research extends the literature by examining how consumer characteristics moderate the persuasive impact of AI- and human-designed ads. Across a pretest and six large-scale experimental studies involving 6,579 consumer evaluations in Japan, this research finds that advertisements with undisclosed AI authorship often outperform human-designed advertisements in enhancing ad perceptions of creativity, credibility, clarity, and mental imagery (i.e., stimulating vivid consumer imagination) and, consequently, increasing purchase intentions. However, AI-generated ads are less effective among consumers with more generative AI experience, higher education, greater product category involvement, and lower interest in science. In these consumer segments, human-designed ads often have the advantage. These findings extend algorithm aversion theory by providing indirect evidence consistent with an implicit mechanism through which consumer characteristics trigger implicit algorithm detection (i.e., sensing algorithmic markers) and implicit algorithm aversion (i.e., subconscious devaluation of perceived artificiality) without requiring explicit disclosure of AI authorship. The findings inform marketing practice by emphasizing the importance of consumer segmentation.

items.title: Incorporación de la temática de inteligencia artificial en programas de formación docente en Uruguay
items.abstract: The popularization of agents, models, and tools incorporating artificial intelligence is a phenomenon that has recently mobilized social and educational spheres due to new ethical and academic considerations, as well as the difficulties that arise when designing and evaluating learning experiences. The purpose of this study was to characterize the meaning and assess the scope of references to Artificial Intelligence (AI) in teacher training programs for secondary education in Uruguay, within the current curriculum (Plan 2023). The study focuses on STEM-related specialties. Through a content analysis of 156 curricular documents, the context of AI references was quantified and interpreted. The results show that these references are given a more instrumental than critical meaning. The presence of the Computer Science Teacher Training specialty is relevant, given that the interdisciplinary nature of the STEM approach can contribute to deepening critical thinking, transversality, and curricular flexibility for the pedagogical inclusion of these emerging technologies in teacher training.

items.abstract: Objective: To examine burnout rates among nursing professionals reported in publications from 2022 to 2026, considering measurement differences, associated factors, and implications for care. Methods: A descriptive narrative literature review based on scientific studies and reviews published within the defined period. Results: A 2023 meta-analysis estimated a global burnout prevalence of 30.0% (95% CI: 26.0–34.0%). A 2025 umbrella review reported a pooled prevalence of 33.45% for emotional exhaustion, 25.0% for depersonalization, and 33.49% for reduced personal accomplishment. A Brazilian study published in 2026 involving 3,594 nursing workers identified moderate exhaustion in 42.29% of participants; this indicator should not be interpreted as an overall syndrome prevalence. Conclusion: Burnout is a major occupational health concern, and heterogeneous measurement approaches require cautious interpretation and organizational prevention.

items.title: Industrial Architecture and Worker Safety
items.abstract: This paper examines industrial architecture and worker safety through a multidisciplinary architectural lens. It considers workflow, daylight, ventilation, ergonomics, and hazard prevention, while linking design choices to user experience, environmental performance, material responsibility and project delivery. The discussion synthesises established architectural literature, design guidance and recognised standards rather than presenting a new empirical survey. It argues that context-sensitive analysis, inclusive design, coordinated technical decisions and post-occupancy evaluation are essential to credible architectural outcomes. The paper concludes with practical directions for design teams and identifies the need for project-specific evidence before generalising strategies across climates, building types or communities.

items.title: Institutionalising Practicum Modules in Tanzania’s Livestock Training System: Institutional Challenges and Implications for Competency-Based Education and Training
items.abstract: Competency-based education and training (CBET) requires graduates to apply knowledge, perform occupational tasks, solve practical problems, and exercise professional judgement in authentic work environments. This narrative review examined the meaning and educational significance of practicum, the relationship between classroom learning and workplace competence, potential implementation barriers, relevant international experiences, and strategies for strengthening practicum in Tanzania’s livestock training system. The review synthesised literature and documentary information on workplace learning, agricultural and technical training, and apprenticeship approaches in Tanzania and selected countries. The findings distinguish theoretical instruction, institution-based practical training, field activities, and structured workplace practicum as complementary but non-equivalent learning experiences. Effective practicum requires clearly defined learning outcomes, authentic occupational tasks, supervised participation, constructive feedback, documented learning, and competency-based assessment. The synthesis identified potential implementation barriers, including inadequate financing, limited placement opportunities, unclear institutional and employer responsibilities, insufficient supervisor preparation, safety and safeguarding concerns, and weak assessment arrangements. International and Tanzanian apprenticeship examples highlighted transferable principles of employer engagement, shared training responsibilities, structured supervision, and quality assurance. However, available evidence does not establish the prevalence of these barriers or the adequacy of practicum across all Tanzanian livestock training institutions. The review proposes a coordinated framework integrating curriculum alignment, approved placement hosts, progressive competency development, student protection, sustainable financing, employer partnerships, and continuous monitoring. Tanzania should establish context-sensitive practicum standards, assess institutional readiness, strengthen collaboration between training institutions and livestock-sector employers, and pilot and evaluate implementation before wider adoption. National empirical research is also needed to establish baseline conditions and assess practicum quality and outcomes. Institutionalising structured practicum could strengthen the relevance of livestock education and support graduate preparedness for employment

items.title: INTEGRATING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND DIGITAL TECHNOLOGIES IN LANGUAGE TEACHING: A PEDAGOGICAL REVIEW
items.abstract: This paper examines the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies into language teaching. It explores their role in developing vocabulary, grammar, pronunciation, writing, and independent learning. The study adopts a literature review approach and uses the SAMR model to discuss technology integration in education. It also highlights challenges such as the reliability of AI-generated feedback, learners’ dependence on AI tools, and unequal access to digital resources. The paper emphasizes that effective technology integration requires clear learning objectives, teacher guidance, and meaningful communication. It concludes that AI and digital technologies should complement, rather than replace, teachers in language education.

items.title: INTEGRATING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND DIGITAL TECHNOLOGIES TO DEVELOP ESP STUDENTS' READING COMPETENCE THROUGH SPECIALIZED TEXTS
items.abstract: This article examines how artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies can be integrated into English for Specific Purposes (ESP) reading instruction using discipline-specific texts. The problem addressed is the mismatch between the linguistic and conceptual demands of authentic professional materials and learners’ varying levels of reading proficiency. A qualitative, literature-based methodological design was employed, combining thematic synthesis of established ESP and reading scholarship with instructional design analysis. The principal result is a three-stage framework linking pre-reading preparation, guided while-reading analysis and post-reading transfer to specific AI-supported teacher actions and observable learning evidence. A worked example demonstrates implementation with a professional text and identifies safeguards for accuracy, privacy and learner autonomy. The framework is a proposed pedagogical model, not an experimentally validated intervention. The article concludes that AI is most useful when it supports purposeful reading, disciplinary meaning-making and teacher-led formative assessment rather than replacing authentic engagement with texts.

items.title: Integrating Artificial Intelligence into Soft Skills Development: Opportunities and Challenges
items.abstract: In the 21st century, soft skills such as communication, critical thinking, teamwork, leadership, problem-solving, and emotional intelligence are essential for personal and professional development. Unlike academic knowledge, they enhance the practical impact of what a person knows. As artificial intelligence (AI) develops rapidly, integrating it into education, and specifically into soft skills development, may accelerate learning. However, few existing solutions bring these skills together in a single system. Many learners prioritize academic knowledge because soft skills are not formally assessed and do not lead to a diploma. As a result, these skills are often neglected, although employers increasingly expect them in both international and domestic settings. This article explores how soft skills development can be combined in a single AI-based system. The pilot study draws on a survey of some respondents. The analysis examines how respondents currently use AI to develop soft skills, which skills they consider the most important and the most difficult to develop, and whether attitudes differ by age or occupation.

items.title: Integrating Foreign Students Through Education for Values
items.abstract: Recognising the challenges that international students face in integrating the Portuguese Education System, NOVA University launched a semester-long Foundation Program in 2017. Within this program, we introduced the Ideas Club course in 2020 to promote students’ engagement and facilitate long-term academic success. This paper examines whether and how the course has helped these students overcome cultural barriers and adapt to the European context. European issues serve as a guiding framework to help non-European students interact and discuss in constructive ways, thereby grasping the complexities of European reality. The course adopts a dialogic pedagogical approach, promoting student-led discussions on diverse topics while encouraging consciousness, critical reflection, and the dismantling of some stereotypes. Literature in international foundation education highlights the importance of self-determination theory in fostering intrinsic motivation, which is essential for the desired engagement and academic success. We show in this paper how the Ideas Club contributes to fostering intrinsic motivation.

items.title: Interactive Multimedia Game-Based Learning (MMI-GBL) to Support Student Engagement and Problem Solving in Elementary Education: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Background: Interactive multimedia and educational games offer opportunities for elementary learning, but their mechanisms and outcome measures are heterogeneous.Aims: To synthesize the design features of interactive multimedia game-based learning (MMI-GBL), the evidence on student engagement, the implications for problem solving, and the methodological limitations of the field.Methods: This systematic literature review follows PRISMA 2020 reporting principles with descriptive mapping and narrative synthesis. A previously compiled 41-reference bibliography was reconciled into a retrospectively defined core set of 17 publications (2022–2026) and 24 supporting references. Core sources comprise seven empirical studies and ten secondary syntheses. Data were entered into a structured extraction matrix and appraised qualitatively by context and outcome construct.Results: Five empirical publications concern elementary or early elementary learners, including one complementary multimedia study, and address mathematics learning, task solving, computing terminology, and engagement. Recurring design features include coherent multimedia representations, explicit goals and missions, adaptive scaffolding, specific feedback, and opportunities to retry and reflect. Designs in which scaffolding and feedback prompted learners to choose strategies, explain, and revise were associated with learning and engagement gains, whereas rewards detached from reasoning contributed little. Behavioral and cognitive engagement were the dimensions most often evidenced; emotional and agentic engagement were rarely measured. Perceived usefulness or achievement does not directly measure problem-solving performance, and external meta-analytic estimates remain contextual.Conclusion: MMI-GBL is most effective when multimedia features, game mechanics, scaffolding, feedback, and teacher facilitation are aligned with meaningful learning activities. Further elementary-level research is needed to strengthen evidence on engagement and problem-solving outcomes.

items.title: Large language models facilitate knowledge extraction for troubleshooting
items.abstract: Troubleshooting in operational environments relies on expert knowledge that is often undocumented and highly contextual. Informal data sources, such as communication logs, may hold some of this information, but their unstructured nature makes interpretation challenging. In a preliminary case study with a telescope operations facility, we explored whether large language models (LLMs) can reconstruct troubleshooting strategies from chat logs. LLM outputs were compared against those produced by a novice human analyst by two expert evaluators. We also compared an LLM with additional technical information in the context window and LLM outputs augmented by another novice analyst. While the domain experts varied in their scoring, overall LLM-generated analyses were judged as higher quality and more accurate than human-produced outputs. Neither additional technical context nor human augmentation resulted in meaningful improvements. These preliminary findings suggest LLMs show promise for expert knowledge extraction and decision-support in operational environments.

items.title: Longitudinal effects of parental mediation strategies on adolescent sexting
items.abstract: Sexting is relatively common behavior among adolescents, yet it raises parental concerns as it may pose substantial risks, particularly when occurring with unknown individuals met online. While parental mediation strategies are often recommended to mitigate such risks, longitudinal evidence for their effectiveness remains limited. To address this gap, our four-wave longitudinal study examines the impact of active and restrictive parental mediation on adolescents’ sending and receiving sexually-oriented online messages, including sexting, with people met online. We also examined adolescents’ age and gender as moderators. We analyzed data from 3,087 Czech adolescents (age M = 13.47, SD = 1.74, 50.1% male) using random intercept cross-lagged panel model. This approach advances understanding of the bidirectional dynamics between parenting and adolescent online sexual risk behaviors. Results show that active mediation was connected to lower sending and receiving such messages on a between-person level. However, on a within-person level, patterns were inconsistent. Increases in active mediation sometimes predicted higher receiving six months later, particularly among older adolescents, but effect was not stable, and no such effects were found for sending. In contrast, restrictive mediation was unrelated to sexting on a between-person level but showed some within-person effects, as at T2 higher restrictions predicted less sending and receiving at T3. Our results show that parental mediation has complex and context-dependent effects. Active mediation seems to reflect the overall communication climate within a family, rather than serving as a direct tool for changing behavior. These findings shift attention from parental mediation as a direct behavior-control strategy toward the broader role of developmentally sensitive family communication in helping adolescents navigate online sexual experiences.

items.title: Measuring and Enhancing Digital-Intelligence Literacy: An Empirical Study in Zhejiang, China
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is accelerating the transformation of digital society from “tool-based application” to “intelligent collaboration,” creating demand for composite competencies in technical operation, ethical awareness, and human–AI collaboration. To address limitations in existing digital literacy frameworks, particularly their inadequate treatment of cognitive overload, ethical risks, and disparities in the depth of GAI use, this study proposes the concept of “digital-intelligence literacy” (DIL) and constructs a comprehensive five-dimensional evaluation framework comprising Data-Inquisitive, Synergistic-Adaptive, Digital-Content-Hermeneutic, Ethico-Security, and Solution-Application literacies. Using 667 stratified random survey samples from Zhejiang Province, China, and employing principal component analysis, one-way ANOVA, structural equation modeling (SEM), and LASSO regression, this study systematically examines the current status, group disparities, and underlying mechanisms of DIL. The findings reveal the following: significant disparities in DIL across age groups, education levels, and GAI usage frequency, with older adults and low-frequency users encountering prominent challenges; GAI cognition emerges as the most critical factor for improving DIL, substantially exceeding the influence of attitudes and environmental perceptions; a core competency transformation chain of “Synergistic-Adaptive → Digital-Content-Hermeneutic → Solution-Application” literacy revealed by SEM, alongside dynamic interaction between safety-ethics and technological exploration; and participation intentions in DIL-related education are primarily driven by existing literacy levels, usage habits, and attitudes rather than cognitive factors alone. Based on these findings, this study proposes a “cognition-first, systemic-empowerment” strategy, including nationwide educational initiatives centered on GAI-based general knowledge and differentiated empowerment strategies for key groups, providing empirical evidence for local governments to formulate precise and inclusive literacy enhancement policies.

items.title: Misconceptions of artificial intelligence: the modern seer as a synthesis of human knowledge without consciousness, emotion, or moral sill
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is often depicted in public discourse as either a compliant statistical instrument or an emerging entity endowed with knowledge, creativity, feelings, and intentions that may soon rival human capabilities. Both portrayals are fundamentally flawed, as they rely solely on observable performance and infer internal experiences from social appearances. This Viewpoint advocates for a more rigorous model: conceptualizing artificial intelligence as a modern seer, an intricate system that compresses, retrieves, and recombines recorded human knowledge at scales unattainable by any individual. The Viewpoint develops the seer from a metaphor into an analytical framework. The seer is a consulted but uncertified epistemic authority: its capabilities generate interaction cues, the cues invite inferences of understanding, emotion, intention, and authority, and governance must act on these cues and on the calibration of trust rather than on claims about a machine mind. This model clarifies both the practical utility of these systems and the misguided authority often attributed to them. It demonstrates that synthesis can generate novel insights without consciousness, that affective language can provide reassurance without genuine concern, and that value-sensitive recommendations can be produced without moral agency. These distinctions do not render the technology inherently safe, as systems lacking experience can still amplify errors, entrench biases, concentrate power, and undertake consequential actions. The field of drug development exemplifies these limitations: a model may integrate evidence throughout the pharmaceutical process; nevertheless, biological validation and accountable judgment remain essential. This discussion is no longer solely philosophical; regulatory bodies such as the United States Food and Drug Administration, the European Medicines Agency, the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors, and prominent scientific publishers have each adopted frameworks to evaluate context, risk, credibility, and transparency, none of which directly address machine consciousness. Institutions have already moved beyond metaphor-based policymaking. This Viewpoint encourages scientists and scholars to do the same. It identifies ten misconceptions, eight category errors and two factual errors, traces each to the interaction cue that produces it, and states what the framework adds to existing debates on anthropomorphism, stochastic parrots, responsibility gaps, and context-based governance. Addressing these misconceptions will change how AI systems are tested, trusted, and governed.

items.title: Mobile Location-Based Recommendation Systems and Local Businesses: Evidence from the Restaurant Industry
items.abstract: When looking for a place to eat, how much do recommendations on your smartphone influence your choice? Can they help restaurants tucked away on side streets thrive in an age of algorithmic recommendations? We studied the launch of a location-based recommendation feature on South Korea’s largest search platform, tracking 16,720 restaurants over eight months. We find that visibility matters, but its benefits are uneven. Restaurants tucked away on side streets, far from subway stops, attracted the most additional attention when recommended by the algorithm. Yet this advantage did not translate into greater intentions to visit. Making a restaurant easier to discover did not necessarily overcome the inconvenience of reaching it. Digital information helped bridge this online-to-offline friction. Hard-to-reach restaurants with stronger online reputations and richer information, including customer reviews, photos, and menus, were better able to turn attention into visit intentions. For small businesses, visibility creates opportunities, but credible information helps turn attention into potential customers. For platforms and policymakers, location-based recommendations can bring overlooked businesses into view, but realizing their potential requires making reliable information readily available to consumers.

items.title: Modeling Steering Times of Oblique 3D Paths
items.abstract: Understanding how users perform steering tasks on planar user interfaces (UIs) presented at oblique angles is important for designing effective interfaces in 3D workspaces such as VR, where the viewer’s angle relative to the content can vary. However, existing steering models have mainly assumed frontal viewing and do not fully account for viewpoint-dependent changes in apparent path geometry. We conducted a VR experiment in which users performed raycasting-based steering on circular paths displayed on a UI plane. We varied the oblique angle ϕ from 0° to 60°. We found that movement time generally increased as ϕ increased, and error rate was significantly higher at 60° than in the 0° , 20° , and 40° conditions. To model this effect, we extended the steering law using apparent path length, apparent width, and projected local curvature computed from the user’s viewpoint. A baseline steering model based only on geometric path length and width on the UI plane achieved an adjusted R 2 of 0.9024, whereas a viewpoint-dependent global steering model based on apparent path length and width achieved an adjusted R 2 of 0.9637. A local curvature-integrated steering model further improved the fit, achieving the highest adjusted R 2 of 0.9910 and the lowest AIC among the compared models. In leave-one-condition-out cross-validation, this model showed the best predictive performance among the compared models. These results show that incorporating how the appearance of geometry changes with the viewpoint improves steering-time prediction in our tested VR setup, which provides quantitative design guidance for spatially fixed UIs.

items.title: Motivations for Corporate Volunteering and Basic Psychological Needs Satisfaction and Frustration at Work: A Study on Employees of Middle‐ and Large‐Sized Companies in Poland
items.abstract: Although large corporations are increasingly implementing corporate volunteering as a strategic corporate social responsibility initiative, the psychological drivers of such participation remain underexplored. Drawing on self‐determination theory and the functional theory approach to volunteering, this study surveyed 440 nonmanagerial employees from medium‐ and large‐sized enterprises in Poland. Our goal was to investigate the link between the satisfaction and frustration of basic psychological needs at work and motivations for corporate volunteering. We used linear regression and latent profile analyses to test our hypotheses. The results showed that relatedness satisfaction was positively associated with all motives recognized by functional theory, except the social motive. Relatedness frustration was also positively related to the protective, career, and enhancement motives. Additionally, latent profile analysis identified three need satisfaction profiles (satisfied, autonomy‐frustrated, and relatedness‐and‐competence frustrated) that varied in their motives for corporate volunteering, except for career motive. We discuss the practical implications for employers and corporate managers interested in implementing or encouraging participation in corporate volunteering programs.

items.title: Navigating sustainability tensions at work: Towards sustainable human performance work systems
items.abstract: Purpose This study develops Sustainable Human Performance Work Systems (SHuPWS) to explain how HR systems can address the tensions created by integrating sustainability into strategic human resource management. Design/methodology A systematic review of 108 Scopus-indexed articles identifies recurring tensions, theoretical perspectives, and sustainability-oriented HR practices. The synthesis integrates stakeholder theory, the resource-based view, and the ability–motivation–opportunity framework across macro, meso, and micro levels. Findings Five interdependent tensions concern short- and long-term priorities, organisational performance and employee well-being, dualistic and paradoxical thinking, autonomy and standardisation, and business-oriented and values-based sustainability. SHuPWS are conceptualised as configurations of interdependent HR practices that connect economic, social and environmental objectives with employee well-being, voice, capability development and sustainable effort. Ability-, motivation- and opportunity-enhancing practices are proposed to influence short- and medium-term processes contributing to triple-bottom-line outcomes. These relationships vary across configurations, time horizons, and institutional and organisational conditions. Originality/value The study advances sustainable HRM research by identifying sustainability tensions within the design and operation of HR systems. The framework incorporates configurational, temporal and contextual variation into the explanation of system effects over time. It connects stakeholder expectations, organisational capabilities and employee experience within a multilevel account, and specifies relationships for subsequent empirical examination.

items.title: Negotiating Creative Agency in AI-Assisted Music Production: Insights from Filipino Music Producers
items.abstract: As generative AI becomes integrated into creative practice, understanding how creative agency is negotiated during human–AI collaboration has become a challenge for Human–Computer Interaction (HCI). This paper reports preliminary findings from a qualitative study involving semi-structured interviews with three Filipino music producers who incorporate generative AI into their workflows. Inductive analysis identified negotiation moments through which participants determined where and how generative AI could participate and how AI-generated contributions should be evaluated, modified, and incorporated. We use negotiation moments as an emerging analytical lens for understanding how creators regulate AI participation while exercising creative agency. Rather than treating AI as an autonomous collaborator or passive tool, participants determined the scope of AI involvement and retained human judgment over how AI contributions became part of their work. These preliminary findings offer an HCI perspective on how creative AI systems might support human decision-making and creative control.

items.title: Neurolinguistic Perspectives on Syntactic Offloading in AI-Assisted Academic Writing
items.abstract: This conceptual study examines potential neurolinguistic mechanisms associated with generative artificial intelligence (GAI)-assisted academic writing and proposes a conceptual model centered on the proposed theoretical construct of syntactic offloading. As large language models (LLMs) increasingly support stages of scholarly text production, traditional cognitive boundaries between internal language generation and external computational support are being redrawn. Grounded in Levelt’s speech production model and Hagoort’s Memory–Unification–Control (MUC) framework, this research examines how delegating sentence construction, grammatical structuring, and discourse organization to AI affects working memory allocation, executive control, and language production networks. The paper conceptualizes syntactic offloading as a specialized form of cognitive offloading in which specific syntactic planning operations are partially transferred to AI systems, while the writer retains agency over conceptualization, critical evaluation, and communicative intent. Under the proposed account, syntactic offloading may redistribute rather than necessarily diminish overall cognitive engagement: working memory demands shift from low-level sentence generation to high-level evaluation, source integration, and scientific verification. Concurrently, executive control functions such as attentional regulation, inhibitory control, and metacognitive monitoring become paramount in assessing AI-generated outputs for conceptual precision, methodological validity, and stylistic alignment. The article further discusses the possible neuroplastic implications of sustained reliance on AI sentence formulation, considering whether long-term syntactic offloading may alter the functional engagement of neural pathways (e.g., Broca’s area (Brodmann area 44, BA44)) responsible for independent syntactic processing. Ultimately, the study frames AI-assisted academic writing as a distributed, bidirectional interaction between human cognition and computational support. It emphasizes the necessity of maintaining human critical oversight to preserve authorial voice and scholarly rigor while leveraging AI for enhanced writing efficiency.

items.title: Not All Students Respond Equally to GAI Guidance: How Field Dependence–Independence Moderates Critical Thinking Behaviors in Human–AI Collaborative Writing
items.abstract: Generative AI (GAI) can support writing, but learners may respond differently to its guidance. This study examined whether field dependence–independence (FDI) moderated the effect of GAI guidance on critical thinking behaviors (CTB) during human–AI collaborative writing. In a mixed-design study, 65 journalism students completed news-writing tasks with Standard GAI, which provided direct responses, and Heuristic GAI, which elicited learners’ reasoning. We coded 696 user prompts as CTB or non-CTB and analyzed them with logistic generalized linear mixed-effects models. Heuristic GAI was associated with more CTB overall, but its effect decreased as GEFT scores increased: students toward the field-dependent end showed larger increases in CTB and greater uptake of cognitive guidance. Source-specific analyses located this heterogeneity primarily in learners’ uptake of cognitive guidance; neither the condition nor moderation effect was significant for learner-initiated CTB. The findings support learner-sensitive GAI scaffolding in educational HCI.

items.title: Organizing critique at critical organizations: Digital transmediality and critical positionality
items.abstract: Critical organizations, whose missions involve producing social critique, such as academic, journalistic, and activist organizations, face what we term a dilemma of “critical positionality,” meaning that they must respond to contradictory demands for critical proximity and distance. This dilemma arises because legitimate critique must remain “close to the ground” to access “lived experiences” yet also adopt sufficient distance from practice to allow for problematization. Critical positionality is an organizational challenge that is exacerbated during moments of digital transitions, when proximity and distance are reconfigured through transmediality—that is, movement of content across media types—which can disrupt organizational practices oriented toward critical positionality. To understand how organizations navigate digital transmediality to maintain their critical positions, we studied a Brazilian progressive news outlet during a digital transition. Organizational attempts to build proximity to users were followed by a reactive attempt at repositioning, which cascaded into further efforts to stabilize a position consistent with the organization’s critical mission. By analyzing approximation and distancing dynamics, we contribute to understanding critical positionality in practice, discussing how critique is shaped by evolving requirements of digital transmediality, and illustrating organizational tensions developed in this process in a critical news outlet.

items.title: Perceived AI agreement and teacher support for reasoned dissent in relation to intellectual humility and counterevidence seeking
items.abstract: Introduction When students feel that generative artificial intelligence (AI) agrees with them, do they remain willing to acknowledge possible error and seek evidence against their own views? We distinguished AI support for an answer from teacher support for questioning an answer. We examined how perceived AI agreement and teacher support for reasoned dissent relate to state intellectual humility and reported counterevidence seeking. Methods We surveyed 386 undergraduates, mainly first-year students, at one vocational and technical university. Students completed the questionnaire in class after an AI-assisted English learning task. A separate pilot sample informed the measurement model. Confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling examined the associations, with bootstrap intervals for indirect associations. Results In the main model, perceived AI agreement and teacher support were positively associated with intellectual humility. Humility was positively associated with reported counterevidence seeking. The estimated indirect associations involving humility were positive for both predictors. Their bootstrap intervals excluded zero, with no clear difference between the two estimates. Neither direct path was statistically significant in the main model. Discussion These initial findings suggest that perceived support for one’s view and encouragement to question claims should be considered together when examining humility and counterevidence seeking in AI-assisted learning.

items.title: Perceived Quality of AI-Enabled Social Media Intelligence and Sustainable Brand Perception: A Sequential Mediation Analysis
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has changed how brands communicate with consumers through personalized recommendations, automated responses, and algorithm-driven content on social media. However, favorable evaluations of these interactions may not directly translate into purchasing intentions or positive brand perceptions. This study examines the relationship between perceived AI-enabled social media intelligence quality and sustainable brand perception through the sequential mediating roles of consumer digital trust, electronic word-of-mouth (e-WOM) intention, and purchase intention. Data were collected from 250 Indonesian social media users and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. The results show that AI-enabled social media intelligence quality is positively associated with digital trust and e-WOM intention. Digital trust is positively associated with e-WOM intention, but its direct relationship with purchase intention is not statistically significant. Both e-WOM intention and purchase intention are positively associated with sustainable brand perception. The hypothesized sequential indirect effect is statistically significant (β = 0.028, p = 0.001). From an information systems perspective, these findings provide empirical evidence linking perceived AI-mediated communication quality to psychological, social, behavioral, and perceptual responses. The study suggests that evaluations of AI-enabled communication systems should consider user trust and recommendation intentions alongside prospective commercial outcomes. Keywords—AI-enabled social media intelligence, digital trust, electronic word-of-mouth, purchase intention, sustainable brand perception, sequential mediation.

The study examines the advantages of adaptive learning platforms, generative language models (LLMs), and automated assessment systems tailored to students' language proficiency levels, learning paces, and individual needs. Furthermore, practical recommendations and methodological approaches for the step-by-step integration of AI tools into the educational framework are presented.
